replicas in ap-southeast-1 and ap-southeast-3, using the default multi-Region eventual consistency mode
merchant_id#idempotency_key, no indexes; replicas in ap-southeast-1 and ap-southeast-3, both writable)

evidence.quote: exactly one request can acquire the lock for a given merchant and key regardless of which
replicas in ap-southeast-1 and ap-southeast-3, using the default multi-Region eventual consistency mode
Payments API in each region reads and writes its local replica

With both replicas writable, each region checking conditions against its local copy, and replication asynchronous, a duplicate arriving in the other region within the lag cannot see the first lock, so two regions can both acquire it; the exact conflict semantics of the global table must be confirmed.

next_step.action: Confirm the DynamoDB global-table conditional-write semantics for the chosen consistency mode, and choose between single-writer routing and a strongly consistent mode before Phase 3.

reassessment.note: Introduced by the v1.1 cross-region replication change (Section 9.4) made in response to prior FND-004.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 9.4, confirm the global-table conditional-write and conflict semantics. Then make the lock single-writer: all lock acquisitions go to the ap-southeast-1 replica, including from the Jakarta cell, until failover is formally declared. Alternatively, adopt a strongly consistent multi-Region mode if the platform offers one for this region pair. Correct the Section 24 entry ('both writable') to match. Verify with a chaos test that sends concurrent duplicates split across both regions and checks that the acquirer simulator records exactly one authorization.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Restores FR-5 (one downstream authorization per merchant and key) during partial outages and regional failover.
recommendation.issue: The cross-region exclusivity of the idempotency lock rests on a conditional write evaluated against an eventually consistent local replica.
recommendation.rationale: Conditional checks on an asynchronously replicated, multi-writer table cannot see in-flight writes from the other region, so exclusivity is not established by the design.
recommendation.verification: Cross-region concurrent-duplicate test added to the FR-5 acceptance criteria in Section 26.1.

findings.statement: Section 9.4 is new in v1.1. It says the conditional put on attribute_not_exists(pk) lets exactly one request take the lock whichever region receives it. However, the table runs in the default multi-Region eventual-consistency mode and each region writes to its own local replica. A conditional write is checked only against the local replica, so during replication lag both Singapore and Jakarta can take the lock, and the platform's conflict resolution then picks one write silently. The claim that a retry routed to Jakarta during a partial Singapore outage is deduplicated is therefore unsupported. If it is wrong, FR-5 (at most one authorization per merchant and key) fails during exactly the failover scenarios this change was meant to cover.
findings.title: Global-table idempotency lock claimed exclusive across regions under eventual consistency

A timeout means the outcome is unknown, not failed; discarding a late approval while cascading leaves a live issuer authorization that the ledger never sees, so the no-duplicate claim does not hold.

reassessment.note: Section 11.2 is unchanged on this point in v1.1. The only edit added the CVC clause.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 11.2, delete the 'cannot create a duplicate charge' sentence. Add a rule: any approval received for a superseded or timed-out attempt triggers an automatic reversal or void through that adapter, recorded on the attempt and audited. For acquirers that support reversals by reference, optionally send a reversal for the timed-out attempt before cascading. Extend the FR-7 cascade simulation with a late-approval injection case.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Prevents double authorizations on customers' cards and keeps P1 (the payment record is the truth) consistent with issuer state; supports FR-7.
recommendation.issue: Timeout outcomes are treated as non-success, and late approvals are discarded without being reversed.
recommendation.rationale: An unknown outcome can be an approval; nothing compensates for one that arrives late.
recommendation.verification: Acquirer simulator returns an approval at 2,600 ms on attempt 1 and approves attempt 2. The test passes when exactly one authorization remains open and a reversal is logged for attempt 1.

findings.statement: Section 11.2 still says cascading cannot create a duplicate charge because the previous attempt did not succeed. Yet a 2,500 ms timeout is classed as retryable, and late responses are 'logged and discarded'. A timed-out attempt may have been approved by the first acquirer, and the cascade can then be approved by a second, leaving two authorizations on the customer's card. The design has no step that reverses the orphaned approval, which conflicts with P1 and with the intent of FR-7.
findings.title: 'Cascading cannot create a duplicate charge' is unsupported for timeout-triggered cascades

doc_anchors.quote: move the p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade
retryable outcomes - soft declines eligible for reattempt plus acquirer-side errors and timeouts - 3.8%.
End-to-end p99 latency for a card authorization, measured at the API edge and including any cascade, shall not exceed 1,500 ms.

evidence.quote: move the p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade
retryable outcomes - soft declines eligible for reattempt plus acquirer-side errors and timeouts - 3.8%.
End-to-end p99 latency for a card authorization, measured at the API edge and including any cascade, shall not exceed 1,500 ms.

If about 3.8% of first attempts are retryable and each triggers a cascade, about 3.8% of card authorizations take the cascade path, which is above 1%, so the p99 falls on cascaded payments. A timeout-then-cascade path costs at least 2,500 ms plus a second round trip, beyond 1,500 ms.

recommendation.change_summary: Rewrite Section 21.1 to model the cascade distribution: share of cascades caused by timeouts versus fast declines, and the per-attempt latency of each. Introduce an overall authorization deadline, for example cascading only if the remaining budget exceeds the next acquirer's p95 round trip, and a shorter attempt timeout for first attempts. Alternatively, bring a governance change to NFR-2 so that it measures cascaded payments separately.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Makes NFR-2 achievable or honestly restated before Phase 9 benchmarking.
recommendation.issue: The p99 budget excludes cascades on a premise contradicted by the document's own baseline.
recommendation.rationale: With cascades inside the p99, the budget in Section 21.1 does not demonstrate that NFR-2 can be met.
recommendation.verification: NFR-2 latency benchmark in Section 26.2 with 3.8% retryable injection, split into the actual timeout and decline mix.

findings.statement: Section 21.1 leaves cascades out of the p99 on the grounds that fewer than 1% of card payments cascade. Section 10.5 reports 3.8% retryable outcomes, and FR-7 cascades every one of them. The cascade path therefore sits inside the p99. Any timeout-triggered cascade alone exceeds 2,500 ms, against the 1,500 ms NFR-2 limit that explicitly includes cascades. The NFR-2 benchmark injects 3.8% retryable outcomes, so the design is likely to fail its own acceptance test.
findings.title: Latency budget's '<1% cascade' premise contradicts the 3.8% retryable baseline

for attempts submitted in the last 60 seconds, and by T+1 reconciliation against settlement lines.

An alert at 4 s does not stop commits whose replication is still pending, so the RPO is a typical value rather than a bound. Recovery that starts from attempt records cannot enumerate attempts whose rows were lost, and cannot query providers that have no status endpoint.

next_step.action: Establish whether Aurora Global Database can enforce an RPO bound, and inventory provider status-API support per adapter.
next_step.owner: Platform SRE lead with Payments Core architect

reassessment.note: v1.1 replaces the infeasible zero regional RPO with ≤5 s, adds the idempotency global table and a provider-status recovery path. The bound and the recovery premise remain unverified.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 20.2, investigate and adopt a mechanism that blocks or throttles commits when global-database lag exceeds the RPO, if Aurora PostgreSQL offers one, or restate NFR-4 as a monitored objective with risk acceptance. Define the recovery source for lost attempts as provider-side search by merchant and time window, the Jakarta idempotency replica's payment_id, or settlement files, independent of the lost rows. Add a per-provider status-API column to the Acquirer Connectivity Matrix. In the NFR-4 game day, measure lag at 2,000 TPS.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Makes the NFR-4 regional RPO and recovery claim true by construction rather than by typical behaviour.
recommendation.issue: The 5-second regional RPO and the loss-window recovery rest on unverified mechanisms.
recommendation.rationale: Without an enforcing mechanism and a recovery source that does not depend on the lost data, NFR-4 cannot be demonstrated.
recommendation.verification: NFR-4 regional game day under 2,000 TPS with an induced replication stall over 5 s: commits are blocked or the breach is detected, and every payment in the window is reconstructed.

findings.statement: v1.1 relaxes NFR-4 to a 5-second regional RPO. However, Section 20.2 only pages when replication lag reaches 4 seconds. Paging does not bound the loss, because asynchronous lag under load or a network partition can exceed 5 seconds. Recovery of the loss window queries provider status APIs 'for attempts submitted in the last 60 seconds'. But the attempt rows that identify those submissions are the data lost in the window, and Section 20.3 concedes that status endpoints exist only 'where one exists'. The claim that every lost payment is recoverable is therefore unsupported for providers without such an endpoint, and for e-wallet and bank flows until T+1.
findings.title: Regional RPO ≤5 s is monitored, not enforced; loss-window recovery assumes records and status APIs that may not exist

reassessment.note: Latent in v1.0. It is made explicit by v1.1's restated NFR-4 ('30 minutes in both cases') and the expanded regional design, which still omits the CDE.

recommendation.change_summary: Add a CDE subsection to Section 20.2 covering: Vault store replication to ap-southeast-3; how KEKs become available there (confirm whether CloudHSM backups can be copied cross-region, and how long a restore takes); Jakarta Card Adapter egress and acquirer allowlisting and certificates; and a DR CDE row in Section 12.2. recommendation.expected_benefit: Makes the NFR-4 RTO credible for card payments and keeps the NFR-5 scope accurate.
recommendation.issue: The regional DR design omits the cardholder data environment.
recommendation.rationale: Card payments depend on the Vault and HSM, so the 30-minute regional RTO cannot hold for cards without a DR CDE.
recommendation.verification: Regional game day completes a card authorization through ap-southeast-3 within 30 minutes of declared failover.

findings.statement: NFR-4 sets a 30-minute RTO for regional loss, and Section 20.2 fails over the API tier and Aurora to ap-southeast-3. The CDE, however, is described only in ap-southeast-1: one HSM in ap-southeast-1a, with backups restorable 'in any AZ'. No Vault data replication, no cross-region key material and no Jakarta Card Adapter connectivity to acquirers is specified. Card authorizations (about 55% of attempts) therefore cannot resume in Jakarta within 30 minutes as written. A DR CDE would also extend the PCI DSS scope defined in Section 12.2.
findings.title: Regional failover assumes card processing in Jakarta, but the CDE (Vault, HSM, Card Adapter) has no cross-region design

recommendation.change_summary: Change Section 12.3 and the Section 24 Vault decision to launch with at least two HSMs in separate AZs. Replace the TPS trigger with a measured utilisation threshold, for example adding an HSM above 50% of benchmarked unwrap capacity. recommendation.expected_benefit: Protects NFR-3 availability and the NFR-1/NFR-2 card throughput at campaign peaks.
recommendation.issue: The HSM scaling trigger is unreachable, and the single HSM is both a throughput and an availability dependency for all card traffic.
recommendation.rationale: The trigger arithmetic contradicts the volume baseline, and no design path removes the single point of failure.

findings.statement: Section 12.3 adds a second HSM only when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS. At the 2027 design peak, card volume is about 1,100 TPS (55% of 2,000), so the trigger never fires within the design horizon. Every detokenise call unwraps a DEK inside that single HSM in ap-southeast-1a. The throughput of one HSM for about 1,100 unwraps per second plus tokenisation and cascades rests only on a 'vendor benchmark'. Its loss stops all card payments, against the 99.95% NFR-3 target. This challenges the approved 'one HSM at launch' decision, based on the document items cited.
findings.title: Single-HSM trigger of 1,500 card TPS will never fire; one-AZ HSM throughput and availability unverified

findings.statement: v1.1 fixes the main defect: CVC is now deleted at the final authorization outcome (TTL 15 minutes), incremental and MIT authorizations no longer use it, and the citation now points to the before-authorization requirements. One premise remains open. The design treats a decline from the first acquirer as not completing authorization, so it can re-present the CVC to a second acquirer. Whether an assessor accepts that reading is not recorded. NFR-5/NFR-6 also name PCI DSS v4.0, which may have been superseded by the time the 2027 assessment takes place; this should be confirmed.
findings.title: CVC held across cascade attempts relies on an undocumented reading of 'completion of authorization'; PCI DSS version cited may be superseded

findings.statement: Section 24 confirms network tokens as the primary card-on-file credential from launch, and Phase 3 includes card-on-file with network tokens marked as not depending on open items.
